# Import required libraries
library(ggplot2) # For data visualization
library(dplyr) # For data manipulation
library(stats) # For statistical functions
library(corrplot) # For correlation plots
library(knitr)


# Import the dataset
# NOTE: update this path to your own working directory before running
USStates <- read.csv("USStates.csv", header=TRUE)

# 1. Given the variables in this dataset, which variables can be considered explanatory (X) and which considered response (Y)?  Can any variables take on both roles?

---
The dataset is miniscule with 50 observations and 13 variables. It covers various demographic features for all 50 states. In my opinion, the "State", "Region", and "Population" variables are demographic as they are either descriptive in nature or too large to be influenced by the other variables. The other variables can all be explanatory variables as they can predict other outcomes (e.g., "College" can predict "HouseholdIncome"). Conversely, we can set the other variables as response variables too (e.g., "HighSchool" to predict "College").

This flexibility is a result of the interconnected nature of these variables. Causality can flow from any direction depending on the question we seek to answer.
---

# Printing the classification table
demographic <- c("State", "Region", "Population")
quantitative <- setdiff(names(USStates), demographic)

var_table <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(USStates),
  Type = ifelse(names(USStates) %in% demographic, "Demographic", "Quantitative"),
  Can_Be_Response = ifelse(names(USStates) %in% c("State", "Region"), "No", "Yes"),
  Can_Be_Explanatory = ifelse(names(USStates) == "State", "No", "Yes")
)

kable(var_table)

# 2. What is the population of interest for this problem (yes this is a trick question!)?

---
Acknowledged that this is a trick question. Our analysis will be restricted to the United States and the dataset contains data on all US states so the sample is the same as the population. Any inferences we make or conclusions we draw will be applicable to the whole country. This is essentially a descriptive analysis but that doesn't mean regression will not be helpful. In fact, it will help us understand the relationships between the variables better.
---

# 3. For the duration of this assignment, let's have HOUSEHOLDINCOME be the response variable (Y). Also, consider STATE, REGION and POPULATION as demographic variables. Obtain basic summary statistics.

# Summary statistics for all variables
num_cols <- sapply(USStates, is.numeric)
num_data <- USStates[, num_cols]

summary_stats <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(num_data),
  n = colSums(!is.na(num_data)),
  Minimum = round(apply(num_data, 2, min, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
  Maximum = round(apply(num_data, 2, max, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
  Mean = round(colMeans(num_data, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
  Median = round(apply(num_data, 2, median, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
  SD = round(apply(num_data, 2, sd, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
)
kable(summary_stats)

# Scatterplots: non-demographic X variables vs HouseholdIncome (Y)
explanatory_vars <- c("HighSchool", "College", "Smokers", "PhysicalActivity", "Obese", "NonWhite", "HeavyDrinkers", "TwoParents", "Insured")

par(mfrow = c(3, 3))
for(var in explanatory_vars) {
  plot(USStates[[var]], USStates$HouseholdIncome, 
       xlab = var, ylab = "HouseholdIncome", 
       main = paste(var, "vs HouseholdIncome"),
       col = "blue", pch = 16)
  abline(lm(HouseholdIncome ~ USStates[[var]], data = USStates), 
         col = "red", lwd = 2)
}

# 4. Obtain all possible pairwise Pearson correlations of the non-demographic variables with Y.

correlations <- data.frame(
  Variable = explanatory_vars,
  Correlation = round(sapply(explanatory_vars, function(var) cor(USStates[[var]], USStates$HouseholdIncome)), 3)
)

correlations <- correlations[order(abs(correlations$Correlation), decreasing = TRUE),]
rownames(correlations) <- NULL
kable(correlations)

---
Based on the scatterplots and correlation coefficients, simple linear regression is appropriate for this data. "College" (r=0.686), "Obese" (r=-0.649), and "Smokers" (r=-0.638) show strong linear relationships with "HouseholdIncome".
---

# 5. Fit Model 1: HouseholdIncome ~ College

Model1 <- lm(HouseholdIncome ~ College, data = USStates)
summary(Model1)

coef_model1 <- coef(Model1)
r_squared <- summary(Model1)$r.squared

cat("Prediction Equation: HouseholdIncome =", round(coef_model1[1], 3), "+", round(coef_model1[2], 3), "* College\n")

# 6. Hypothesis tests for Model 1: T-tests for parameters, F-test/ANOVA for overall model.

model_summary <- summary(Model1)
coef_table <- model_summary$coefficients

cat("T-test Results:\n")
cat("Intercept: t =", round(coef_table[1, "t value"], 3), 
    ", p-value =", format.pval(coef_table[1, "Pr(>|t|)"], digits = 3), "\n")
cat("College: t =", round(coef_table[2, "t value"], 3), 
    ", p-value =", format.pval(coef_table[2, "Pr(>|t|)"], digits = 3), "\n")

anova_table <- anova(Model1)
print(anova_table)

# 7. Compute predicted values, residuals, SSE, SST, SSR, and manual R-squared for Model 1; verify against ANOVA table.

Y_hat_college <- predict.lm(Model1, USStates)
Y <- USStates$HouseholdIncome
residuals_college <- Y - Y_hat_college

SSE_college <- sum(residuals_college^2)
Y_bar_college <- mean(Y)
SST_college <- sum((Y - Y_bar_college)^2)
SSR_college <- sum((Y_hat_college - Y_bar_college)^2)
R_squared_manual <- SSR_college / SST_college

cat("R-squared (manual calculation):", round(R_squared_manual, 4), "\n")
cat("Verification: SSR + SSE =", round(SSR_college + SSE_college, 4), "should equal SST =", round(SST_college, 4), "\n")

# 8. Standardize residuals (without using lm() residuals) and plot histogram + scatterplot vs predicted values.

standardized_residuals_college <- residuals_college / sd(residuals_college)

par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
hist(standardized_residuals_college, 
     main = "Histogram of Standardized Residuals (Model 1: College)", 
     xlab = "Standardized Residuals", col = "lightblue", breaks = 10)

plot(Y_hat_college, standardized_residuals_college, 
     main = "Standardized Residuals vs Predicted Values (Model 1: College)",
     xlab = "Predicted HouseholdIncome", ylab = "Standardized Residuals",
     col = "blue", pch = 16)
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2)

# 9. Fit Model 2 with a different explanatory variable ("Obese") and compare to Model 1.

Model2 <- lm(HouseholdIncome ~ Obese, data = USStates)
summary(Model2)

Y_hat_obese <- predict.lm(Model2, USStates)
residuals_obese <- Y - Y_hat_obese
r_squared_model_obese <- summary(Model2)$r.squared

standardized_residuals_obese <- residuals_obese / sd(residuals_obese)

par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
hist(standardized_residuals_obese, main = "Histogram of Standardized Residuals (Model 2: Obese)", 
     xlab = "Standardized Residuals", col = "lightblue", breaks = 10)
plot(Y_hat_obese, standardized_residuals_obese, 
     main = "Standardized Residuals vs Predicted Values (Model 2: Obese)",
     xlab = "Predicted HouseholdIncome", ylab = "Standardized Residuals", col = "blue", pch = 16)
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2)

# 10. Fit Model 3 (any choice of X/Y) — used "Insured" to predict HouseholdIncome.

Model3 <- lm(HouseholdIncome ~ Insured, data = USStates)
summary(Model3)

Y_hat_Insured <- predict.lm(Model3, USStates)
residuals_Insured <- Y - Y_hat_Insured
r_squared_model_Insured <- summary(Model3)$r.squared

standardized_residuals_Insured <- residuals_Insured / sd(residuals_Insured)

par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
hist(standardized_residuals_Insured, main = "Histogram of Standardized Residuals (Model 3: Insured)", 
     xlab = "Standardized Residuals", col = "lightblue", breaks = 10)
plot(Y_hat_Insured, standardized_residuals_Insured, 
     main = "Standardized Residuals vs Predicted Values (Model 3: Insured)",
     xlab = "Predicted HouseholdIncome", ylab = "Standardized Residuals", col = "blue", pch = 16)
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2)

# Final comparative visuals of actual vs predicted values across all three models
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(Y, Y_hat_college, main = "Model 1: Actual vs Predicted (College)",
     xlab = "Actual HouseholdIncome", ylab = "Predicted HouseholdIncome", col = "blue", pch = 16)
abline(0, 1, col = "red", lwd = 2)

plot(Y, Y_hat_obese, main = "Model 2: Actual vs Predicted (Obese)",
     xlab = "Actual HouseholdIncome", ylab = "Predicted HouseholdIncome", col = "darkgreen", pch = 16)
abline(0, 1, col = "red", lwd = 2)

plot(Y, Y_hat_Insured, main = "Model 3: Actual vs Predicted (Insured)",
     xlab = "Actual HouseholdIncome", ylab = "Predicted HouseholdIncome", col = "darkgreen", pch = 16)
abline(0, 1, col = "red", lwd = 2)
